analysis.one_liner: Would hand TransCanada congressional approval to build Keystone XL, bypassing presidential permitting and further environmental review.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote in any House committee and died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would declare that Congress, using its power over commerce with foreign nations, approves the Keystone XL oil pipeline at the Canadian border on TransCanada's behalf. TransCanada would no longer need a permit from the State Department or any new environmental study; the government's existing review would count as final, and any court challenge would go to a single court in Washington. Construction in Nebraska could not start until the state submitted its own route.
analysis.who_benefits: TransCanada would get what it had been waiting on since 2008: a legislated green light without a presidential permit decision. Canadian oil sands producers and Gulf Coast refiners would gain a pipeline to move heavy crude. Construction workers would get temporary pipeline jobs.

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes TransCanada Keystone Pipeline, L.P. to build, connect, operate, and maintain the border-crossing pipeline facilities under its 2008 application, and says no presidential border permit and no new environmental impact statement are required [S2][S3].

Declares the State Department's August 2011 environmental review sufficient under the National Environmental Policy Act and any other law requiring federal review, and says carrying out the act itself is not a major federal action needing an environmental study [S2][S3].
Confines all court challenges over the pipeline and its permits to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, a single court, instead of lawsuits anywhere along the route [S2][S3].
Withholds construction in Nebraska until the state submits its own route, effectively giving Nebraska control over the in-state path after objections to the original Sand Hills route [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Communities, landowners, and water resources along the route would bear spill and construction risk with the normal federal environmental review process declared complete and challenges limited to one court. The public would lose the standard check of a presidential permitting decision on a foreign oil crossing. Wider costs from expanded oil sands refining fall on air and climate, outside the bill's scope.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes the ordinary checks: no border permit, no further environmental review, and lawsuits funneled to one court, so a legislatively blessed project could not be second-guessed through the normal process [S2][S3].

The bill's job-creation findings are Congress's own assertions; independent estimates at the time put permanent employment near zero, with most work being temporary construction jobs, so the public benefit is much smaller than the title suggests [S3].
Even the bill's strongest safeguard for opponents — waiting for Nebraska's route — waives any federal environmental study of the new route once Nebraska submits it [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The concrete gains are a pipeline permit for one company and a few thousand temporary construction jobs. The costs are structural: Congress substituting its own approval for the executive permitting and environmental review process, shielding the decision from ordinary court challenges, and locking in a route whose remaining review the bill declares unnecessary. For anyone not employed building the pipeline or shipping crude through it, the tradeoff is poor.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees on the day it was introduced and split among subcommittees, none of which ever reported it, so it died quietly when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced on February 9, 2012, and referred the same day to the Transportation and Infrastructure, Energy and Commerce, Natural Resources, and Foreign Affairs Committees [S1][S5].

Within days and over the following months it was sent to the Energy and Power, Railroads Pipelines and Hazardous Materials, Terrorism Nonproliferation and Trade, and Western Hemisphere subcommittees; no committee or subcommittee ever reported it, and no vote ever occurred [S5].
It carried 63 cosponsors, 61 Republicans and 2 Democrats, but that support never translated into committee action before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S4][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained a windfall from the bill dying. TransCanada lost its shot at a statutory shortcut but remained free to pursue its permit through the normal executive process, and communities along the route kept the standard environmental review the bill would have shut off.

for.name: Connie Mack
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to approve Keystone XL by statute and recruited cosponsors.

for.name: 2 of 193 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only Democratic support it drew.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure, Energy and Commerce, Natural Resources, and Foreign Affairs Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and never reported it out, keeping it off the floor.

against.name: President Obama
against.what_they_did: Had denied the Keystone XL permit in January 2012 pending a new Nebraska route review, the decision this bill sought to override by statute; he never considered signing it because it never reached his desk.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was overwhelmingly Republican, 61 of 63, with just two Democrats; opposition came from inaction rather than a recorded vote, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.note: The bill would give one company a legislated construction permit, declare existing review complete, bar any new environmental study, and funnel all lawsuits to a single court. The company's gain comes from removing exactly the review processes the public would otherwise rely on.

A completed Keystone XL would give oil sands crude a direct route to U.S. Gulf Coast refineries, expanding production economics. The public's stake is mainly in the climate and spill risks that the bill's shortcut leaves unexamined.

Refiners along the Gulf Coast sought heavy Canadian crude that the pipeline would deliver. Cheaper crude input helps them but does little for consumers at the pump, since Gulf product largely serves export markets.
Pipeline approval would divert crude that otherwise moves by rail tank car, shrinking that business. Anyone worried about oil train derailments in towns along rail lines loses nothing here.
